That film was that rare thing in the modern movie era: a meticulously crafted drama that was both a huge commercial success (taking in $446 million at the global box office) and an awards darling (it was nominated for 10 Oscars and won three). And it lived and died by MacKay’s performance—as a British soldier sent on an apparent suicide mission across enemy lines at the sharp end of WWI, the camera tracks him for the entire run time. It fell upon him to perfectly sell the emotion—and, perhaps more difficult, the active repression of emotion—brought on by the horrors he’s living through.

Watching that movie in a packed cinema in 2019, I felt like I was witnessing the ascension of another massive British movie star. But MacKay’s role choices in the six years afterwards read more like someone trying to hide from the spotlight than embrace it. As we arrive at the kiosk in the center of the park, after he insists on paying for my coffee (which actually did taste so good), I ask him what has been guiding his career decisions since then.
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa985dc206eb9257891e371/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/George-MacKay-Web-WM-9.jpg

There are two sides to it, he explains, as we sit opposite each other on picnic benches. As the film was set up to look like two long, continuous shots, it required a hell of a lot of planning and constant collaboration with every department. “We rehearsed for four months, and most days we’d rehearse the scene and then the key grip would come in, the head of makeup, the head of costume, Roger Deakins, director of photography…. And they would discuss how we achieved that shot. And I got to be party to those discussions,” MacKay says. “To be inside the filmmaking process as an actor, it was so mind-expanding and fascinating and brilliant.”

On the other side, there was his first brush with all the trappings of a major movie rollout. The publicity tour and the awards circuit that followed were unlike anything he’d experienced before—and it also took him out of actually filming anything for a while. “That’s the longest that I wasn’t on a film set,” MacKay says. “When it looked like you were busier than ever because you’re doing talk shows, and there’s posters and there’s awards talk and all that kind of stuff.”

Over email, Tom Ford describes him as “the kindest and most considerate person on set. Not only to the other actors, but to the crew. The entire production team fell in love with him. I’m afraid that I did too.”

Edgar-Jones has a similar perspective. “I remember watching him learn a TikTok dance with Bodhi, who played little Margaret, for hours,” she says. “He always made the effort to introduce himself to absolutely everyone on set and thank them after each day. Every set is better with George there.”

blocks.x: As we begin our walk back toward our starting point, I notice MacKay bending down to pick stuff up off the ground. He does it so fast that I barely register it at first. But then he does it again, and I realize that he’s collecting garbage—a candy wrapper here, a plastic bottle cap there—and putting it in his pocket to later deposit in the trash can. It makes sense then that MacKay found resonance in Edward, a man who puts propriety above his own happiness. “In Jane Austen and then [screenwriter] Diana Reid’s interpretation of the story, you get someone that really cares about the ‘trash’ that they leave behind,” he says. “So I really revered that selflessness in Edward.”

So, what changed for MacKay to precipitate his return to the mainstream? Somewhat ironically for a man who spent the wee hours performing to no one, it has a lot to do with an audience. As the father of two young children, he has started going to the cinema more, to watch movies aimed at broad crowds. “I maybe previously have considered the filmmaker above the audience, about it being about a personal process, or filmmaker over everything,” he says. “Going to the cinema again I’m like, oh no, I’m an audience member. I want to be entertained.”

It’s not so much about throwing everything he learned from years in indie cinema away, but finding that middle ground between art and entertainment once again. Sense and Sensibility does it beautifully. The Ocean’s Eleven prequel certainly will too. Margot Robbie and her production company, Lucky Chap, I suggest, have proven their ability to turn auteur-driven movies into blockbusters with the likes of Barbie and Saltburn. ”It really is such a beautiful mix of these auteur visions for a mass audience,” MacKay agrees. “And all with something to say as well. Not just for the trickery of like, let’s get Spielberg to do a Marvel.”
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa985dceef4ffb082fcde80/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/George-MacKay-Web-WM-8.jpg
blocks.c: George MacKay walking on a London street

blocks.x: Coat, pants, belt, and scarf (worn at waist) by Celine. Sweater by Prada. Boots by Manolo Blahnik.

Cry to Heaven, on the other hand, is more likely to skew toward the artier side of things. The film is based on the novel of the same name by Anne Rice, about castrato opera singers in 18th-century Italy. But how closely Ford will stick to the text is unclear, as is MacKay’s role. “I can’t say too much, but it’s a wonderful character within it,” he says. I can tell MacKay is keen to pay due respect to Ford and let all that information unfurl when his director wants it to. He won’t confirm if he got to work with Adele, who will feature in her first acting role, or whether the movie is indeed set in the same era as the book, saying only, “I think it will look extraordinary.” Ford, he says, stands out from other directors for his “strength and clarity of vision.” But he is hesitant to go into much detail about his blossoming friendship with Ford, who, the weekend prior to our meeting, had taken MacKay as his guest to Wimbledon. Ford is less anxious, later telling me: “I cannot wait to work with him again, and I believe that we have become true friends.”

As we approach the park gate where MacKay and I get ready to part ways, he brings up the balance he’s been working on—deciding whether to do a movie because it’ll give him a great personal experience or teach him about himself, versus considering its potential impact on an audience or box office appeal. The internal versus the external motivation. He’s still trying to figure it out. “It’s just a very human thing, isn’t it?” he says. “To constantly be recalibrating, how much is for the outer world, how much is for me? And also that’s a constant question that I think is never going to have a fixed answer.”

And then, maybe in part because he’s been basking in the outdoors for several hours, he brings it back to the natural world. “Some of the time the question is like, well, if I stay put, be a rock in the river and it all goes round, how does that work?” he says. “Or actually, do you just go with the current for a little bit, and where do you end up?”

Margot Robbie and her production company, Lucky Chap, I suggest, have proven their ability to turn auteur-driven movies into blockbusters with the likes of Barbie and Saltburn. ”It really is such a beautiful mix of these auteur visions for a mass audience,” MacKay agrees. “And all with something to say as well. Not just for the trickery of like, let’s get Spielberg to do a Marvel.”

Coat, pants, belt, and scarf (worn at waist) by Celine. Sweater by Prada. Boots by Manolo Blahnik.

Cry to Heaven, on the other hand, is more likely to skew toward the artier side of things. The film is based on the novel of the same name by Anne Rice, about castrato opera singers in 18th-century Italy. But how closely Ford will stick to the text is unclear, as is MacKay’s role. “I can’t say too much, but it’s a wonderful character within it,” he says. I can tell MacKay is keen to pay due respect to Ford and let all that information unfurl when his director wants it to. He won’t confirm if he got to work with Adele, who will feature in her first acting role, or whether the movie is indeed set in the same era as the book, saying only, “I think it will look extraordinary.” Ford, he says, stands out from other directors for his “strength and clarity of vision.” But he is hesitant to go into much detail about his blossoming friendship with Ford, who, the weekend prior to our meeting, had taken MacKay as his guest to Wimbledon. Ford is less anxious, later telling me: “I cannot wait to work with him again, and I believe that we have become true friends.”

As we approach the park gate where MacKay and I get ready to part ways, he brings up the balance he’s been working on—deciding whether to do a movie because it’ll give him a great personal experience or teach him about himself, versus considering its potential impact on an audience or box office appeal. The internal versus the external motivation. He’s still trying to figure it out. “It’s just a very human thing, isn’t it?” he says. “To constantly be recalibrating, how much is for the outer world, how much is for me? And also that’s a constant question that I think is never going to have a fixed answer.”

And then, maybe in part because he’s been basking in the outdoors for several hours, he brings it back to the natural world. “Some of the time the question is like, well, if I stay put, be a rock in the river and it all goes round, how does that work?” he says. “Or actually, do you just go with the current for a little bit, and where do you end up?”
